source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A minor insertion-site bruise that needs no reassessment despite increasing pain and swelling","B":"A reason to increase the infusion rate so the remaining phenytoin enters the vein more quickly","C":"Purple glove syndrome, requiring the phenytoin infusion to stop and the site to be evaluated","D":"An expected local phenytoin effect that can be ignored when distal color and swelling develop"}}
source_row.rationale: "Purple glove syndrome" is a rare but serious soft tissue injury associated with IV phenytoin administration, characterized by pain, edema, and purple-bluish discoloration at or distal to the injection site, sometimes occurring even without extravasation. Risk is reduced by administering phenytoin slowly (not exceeding facility/manufacturer-specified maximum rates) through a large-bore IV in a large vein. If suspected, the infusion should be stopped and the provider notified promptly.

source_row.rationale: Isoniazid carries a risk of hepatotoxicity, which can range from mild transaminase elevation to severe, potentially fatal hepatitis. source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Oral vancomycin has poor systemic absorption and stays mainly in the gut, while IV reaches blood","B":"The route differs only because oral vancomycin is cheaper than intravenous vancomycin therapy","C":"Oral and intravenous vancomycin produce essentially identical drug exposure throughout the body","D":"Using oral vancomycin for intestinal infection is a prescribing error because all therapy is IV"}}
source_row.rationale: Oral vancomycin is poorly absorbed systemically, remaining largely within the GI tract, making it ideal for treating C. difficile colitis, a local GI infection. In contrast, IV vancomycin is required to achieve adequate systemic drug levels needed to treat a systemic infection, such as a MRSA bloodstream infection, since oral vancomycin would not reach therapeutic levels outside the gut.

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Flushing with tap water instead of a sterile solution, in order to more effectively clear whatever might be causing this resistance","B":"A push-pause technique, stopping if resistance is ever met, rather than pushing harder as the colleague is currently suggesting","C":"Forceful, rapid flushing without much regard for the resistance felt, similar to what the colleague is currently suggesting doing","D":"Fairly little flushing being needed for this particular device, contrary to why the nurse is performing this task in the first place"}}
source_row.rationale: Proper technique for flushing an intermittent IV access device (heparin/saline lock) includes using a "push-pause" method with an appropriate sterile flush solution (per facility protocol, which may include normal saline alone or with heparin), and stopping immediately if resistance is met — never forcing a flush against resistance, since this could dislodge a clot or cause other complications.
source_row.source_detail: IV access flushing: use prescribed sterile flush technique and never force against resistance; reviewed 2026-08-14.

source_row.rationale: Standard precautions require eye protection (goggles or a face shield) whenever a procedure or activity carries a reasonably anticipated risk of blood or body fluid splash or spray to the face, protecting the mucous membranes of the eyes from potential pathogen exposure, in addition to other appropriate PPE such as gloves and a mask/gown as indicated.

source_row.rationale: Between-case environmental cleaning and disinfection reduces contamination of high-touch and procedure-area surfaces and is one component of infection prevention. It complements rather than replaces aseptic and sterile technique.

source_row.rationale: Correct alcohol-based hand sanitizer technique involves applying enough product to cover all surfaces of the hands and rubbing them together until completely dry (generally taking about 20 seconds), without rinsing or wiping with a towel, which would remove the antimicrobial effect. Visibly soiled hands should be washed with soap and water rather than relying on alcohol-based sanitizer alone.

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Sterilization and disinfection are interchangeable processes with the same microbial endpoint","B":"Sterilization applies only to environmental surfaces and is not used for reusable instruments","C":"Sterilization removes fewer microorganisms than high-level disinfection used on medical devices","D":"Sterilization destroys all microbial life, including bacterial spores, unlike disinfection"}}
source_row.rationale: Sterilization destroys all forms of microbial life, including highly resistant bacterial spores, representing the highest level of microbial elimination — used for items requiring the highest level of safety (such as surgical instruments). Disinfection eliminates most pathogenic microorganisms but does not reliably destroy all bacterial spores, making it appropriate for a different category of items/surfaces based on their intended use and infection risk (per the Spaulding classification).

source_row.rationale: Professional accountability refers to a nurse's acceptance of responsibility for their own actions, clinical decisions, and the outcomes of those decisions, a foundational concept in professional nursing practice reflected in codes of ethics, scope of practice standards, and licensure requirements.

source_row.rationale: Incorporating current nursing research findings into clinical decision-making and protocol development reflects the value of evidence-based practice, helping ensure that nursing care and unit protocols are grounded in the most current, effective, and safe standards of care, rather than relying solely on tradition or personal experience.

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Compensation can preserve near-normal blood pressure through tachycardia and vasoconstriction early","B":"Early shock usually produces bradycardia while blood pressure remains normal through compensation","C":"Compensatory mechanisms do not affect heart rate, vascular tone, or perfusion in the early stage","D":"Severe hypotension must already be present before shock can exist or require clinical recognition"}}
source_row.rationale: In the compensatory (early) stage of shock, the body's compensatory mechanisms (such as tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction) are still able to maintain a relatively normal blood pressure, though subtle signs of hypoperfusion (such as mild tachycardia, anxiety, or slightly delayed capillary refill) may be present, requiring vigilant assessment to detect shock before progression to the decompensated stage, where hypotension becomes evident.

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Full-thickness (third-degree) burn affecting all layers","B":"Partial-thickness burn with blistering and significant pain","C":"A burn with no clinical classification system available","D":"Superficial (first-degree) burn affecting only the epidermis"}}
source_row.rationale: A partial-thickness (second-degree) burn involves the epidermis and part of the dermis, characteristically presenting with blistering, redness, and significant pain (since nerve endings remain intact), distinct from superficial (first-degree) burns (epidermis only, no blistering) and full-thickness (third-degree) burns (through the full dermis, often with reduced pain due to nerve destruction).
source_row.source_detail: Burn depth: partial-thickness injury extends into dermis and commonly blisters and is painful; reviewed 2026-08-14.

source_row.rationale: Traditional frostbite grading is assessed after rewarming. First-degree injury is superficial and does not produce blisters; clear or milky blisters indicate second-degree injury, while hemorrhagic blisters or deeper tissue involvement indicate more severe frostbite.
source_row.source_detail: Frostbite grading after rewarming: first degree has no blisters; second degree clear/milky blisters; deeper grades have hemorrhagic/deep injury; reviewed 2026-08-14.
source_row.source_name: Wilderness Medical Society — Frostbite Classification and Staging
source_row.stem: After rewarming, a client with frostbite has erythematous, mildly edematous skin without blister formation or deeper tissue injury. How is this injury best classified?

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A permanent loss of consciousness that does not resolve spontaneously without resuscitation","B":"A transient complete loss of consciousness with rapid spontaneous and complete recovery","C":"A disorder unrelated to cerebral perfusion that presents primarily with persistent focal deficits","D":"Lightheadedness without actual loss of consciousness, which describes presyncope rather than syncope"}}
source_row.rationale: Syncope is defined as a transient, complete loss of consciousness and postural tone due to temporarily reduced cerebral blood flow, typically with rapid, spontaneous, and complete recovery — distinct from near-syncope (presyncope), which involves the sensation of impending loss of consciousness (lightheadedness, graying vision) without an actual complete loss of consciousness.
source_row.source_detail: Syncope definition: transient loss of consciousness from cerebral hypoperfusion with rapid spontaneous complete recovery; reviewed 2026-08-14.
source_row.source_name: American College of Cardiology / AHA — Syncope Evaluation Guidelines
source_row.stem: A nurse is differentiating between syncope and near-syncope for a client who reports a brief episode of lightheadedness but insists they never actually lost consciousness. The nurse understands that syncope specifically involves:

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Brief position-triggered vertigo without focal neurologic deficits, a pattern that is typical of BPPV here rather than a central neurologic cause.","B":"Continuous vertigo with new dysarthria and unilateral weakness, a pattern that raises concern for a central neurologic cause rather than BPPV.","C":"Persistent vertigo unrelated to head position with new limb ataxia, a pattern that raises concern for a central cause rather than typical BPPV.","D":"Vertigo accompanied by new diplopia and facial weakness, a pattern that requires evaluation for a central neurologic cause rather than typical BPPV."}}
source_row.rationale: BPPV characteristically causes brief, recurrent, position-triggered vertigo. Focal neurologic findings such as dysarthria, weakness, diplopia, or marked limb ataxia are not typical of BPPV and should prompt evaluation for a central cause.
source_row.source_detail: AAO-HNSF 2017 BPPV guideline update: diagnostic criteria and differentiation of BPPV from other causes of imbalance/dizziness; 2026 AAO32 measure continues to cite this CPG. 2017 guideline; current AAO-HNS 2026 quality-measure support rechecked 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: American Academy of Otolaryngology — Peripheral vs. Central Vertigo Distinction
source_row.stem: A client has brief episodes of spinning vertigo triggered by rolling over in bed or turning the head, with no dysarthria, focal weakness, or other neurologic deficit. Which finding is most consistent with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)?

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Vestibular migraine, which can cause episodic vertigo but does not require the characteristic fluctuating hearing loss and aural fullness described here.","B":"Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which usually causes brief position-triggered attacks without the same fluctuating auditory symptom pattern.","C":"Vestibular neuritis, which more often causes a prolonged acute vertigo syndrome without recurrent fluctuating hearing loss and aural fullness.","D":"Ménière's disease, which classically causes recurrent episodic vertigo with fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness."}}
source_row.rationale: The classic symptom tetrad of Ménière's disease includes recurrent episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and a sensation of aural (ear) fullness, resulting from abnormal fluid buildup in the inner ear, warranting evaluation by an ENT specialist for diagnosis and management.
source_row.source_detail: AAO-HNSF Clinical Practice Guideline: Ménière’s Disease, diagnostic key action statement and defining symptom complex. Published 2020-04-08; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: American Academy of Otolaryngology — Ménière's Disease Diagnostic Criteria
source_row.stem: A client reports recurrent episodes of vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, and a sensation of ear fullness, and a family member assumes these are just unrelated random symptoms with no single connecting cause. The nurse should recognize this classic symptom cluster as consistent with:

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A systolic pressure rise of at least 20 mm Hg within 3 minutes of standing, regardless of whether symptoms occur during the position change.","B":"A diastolic pressure rise of at least 10 mm Hg within 3 minutes of standing, regardless of whether symptoms occur during the position change.","C":"Any fall in systolic or diastolic pressure immediately after sitting up, even when the decrease is smaller than established diagnostic thresholds.","D":"A sustained fall of at least 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing from a supine position during upright posture."}}
source_row.rationale: Orthostatic hypotension is defined by a sustained fall in blood pressure of at least 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing (or head-up tilt) from the supine position. Symptoms can support the clinical assessment but are not required for the blood-pressure criterion.
source_row.source_detail: AHA Scientific Statement, definition section: sustained SBP decrease ≥20 mm Hg or DBP decrease ≥10 mm Hg within 3 minutes of standing. Hypertension. 2024; DOI 10.1161/HYP.0000000000000236; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: American Autonomic Society / AAN — Orthostatic Hypotension Diagnostic Criteria
source_row.stem: A nurse evaluates a client for orthostatic hypotension after dizziness on standing. Which blood pressure change meets the standard diagnostic definition in an adult?

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A mild cutaneous allergic reaction that can be observed first because hoarseness and throat tightness do not indicate airway involvement.","B":"Impending upper-airway compromise from anaphylaxis, requiring immediate intramuscular epinephrine and rapid airway assessment.","C":"An isolated anxiety response that can be treated with reassurance before any medication is considered for the allergic reaction.","D":"A delayed gastrointestinal manifestation of allergy that is unlikely to progress to respiratory or cardiovascular compromise."}}
source_row.rationale: Hoarseness and throat tightness in the context of an allergic reaction are concerning early signs of laryngeal edema and impending airway obstruction, a life-threatening feature of anaphylaxis. This requires immediate intervention, including prompt epinephrine administration (the first-line treatment) and preparation for possible advanced airway management if the airway continues to compromise.
source_row.source_detail: WAO Anaphylaxis Guidance 2020, diagnostic criteria Table 2 and acute-management section: laryngeal symptoms and IM epinephrine first-line. 2020 guidance; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: World Allergy Organization — Anaphylaxis Airway Compromise Recognition
source_row.stem: A client experiencing an early anaphylactic reaction develops hoarseness and a sensation of throat tightness. The nurse should recognize these findings as concerning signs of:

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"About 10 to 20 breaths per minute, which is closer to a typical resting adult range than to the expected newborn range.","B":"About 30 to 60 breaths per minute at rest, which is the expected respiratory range for a healthy newborn in routine assessment.","C":"About 60 to 90 breaths per minute at rest, which would be above the usual newborn range and warrants further clinical assessment.","D":"Fewer than 10 breaths per minute at rest, which would be abnormally low rather than an expected newborn respiratory rate."}}
source_row.rationale: Normal newborn respiratory rate is generally higher than the adult range, approximately 30-60 breaths/min, gradually decreasing toward the adult range (approximately 12-20 breaths/min) as the child grows older, reflecting normal age-related physiological differences.
source_row.source_detail: Pediatrics 2016 population-based term-newborn vital-sign study: respiratory-rate centiles during the first days after birth, with lower centiles near 30 and upper centiles near 60 breaths/min after initial transition. Pediatrics 2016;137(4):e20152326; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — Normal Newborn Vital Sign Ranges
source_row.stem: A nurse is assessing the respiratory rate of a healthy newborn. The nurse understands that normal newborn respiratory rate is generally:

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Resting heart rate is generally lowest in infancy and rises gradually through childhood before reaching the adult range.","B":"Resting heart rate remains essentially unchanged from infancy through adulthood when the person is healthy and afebrile.","C":"Resting heart rate is generally higher in infants and young children and decreases toward the usual adult range with age.","D":"Resting heart rate is generally higher in healthy adults than in infants because cardiac output requirements increase with age."}}
source_row.rationale: Normal heart rate is generally higher in infants and young children compared to adults, gradually decreasing toward the typical adult range (about 60-100 beats/min) as the child grows older, reflecting normal age-related physiological changes in cardiovascular function.
source_row.source_detail: 2025 PALS Digital Reference Card, Vital Signs in Children table: age-specific normal heart-rate ranges from infancy through adolescence. Updated to 2025 AHA CPR/ECC science; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) — Age-Based Normal Heart Rate Ranges
source_row.stem: A nurse is comparing normal heart rate ranges across the lifespan. The nurse understands that, in general:

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Lower cardiometabolic risk overall because abdominal adiposity is less clinically relevant than total body weight when BMI is normal.","B":"No additional risk information once BMI is known, because waist circumference does not reflect central fat distribution.","C":"Improved insulin sensitivity and lower vascular risk because a larger waist usually reflects greater lean abdominal mass.","D":"Higher cardiometabolic risk because greater waist circumference reflects central adiposity that can add risk information beyond BMI."}}
source_row.rationale: An elevated waist circumference (reflecting central/abdominal adiposity) is associated with increased cardiovascular and metabolic risk (including risk for type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome), since abdominal fat distribution is associated with greater health risk compared to fat distributed in other body areas, making waist circumference a useful adjunct to BMI in cardiovascular risk assessment.
source_row.source_detail: 2026 CKM guideline, adiposity assessment recommendations: assess BMI and waist circumference because waist provides complementary information about excess-adiposity risk. JACC 2026; DOI 10.1016/j.jacc.2026.03.056; reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: American Heart Association — Waist Circumference and Cardiovascular Risk
source_row.stem: A nurse measures a client's waist circumference as part of a cardiovascular risk assessment, and the client, who has a normal BMI, assumes this measurement won't add anything meaningful beyond what BMI already shows. An elevated waist circumference is instead associated with:

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Normal lower-extremity arterial perfusion because ankle pressure should normally be substantially lower than brachial pressure.","B":"Venous insufficiency rather than arterial disease because ABI is designed primarily to assess venous return from the legs.","C":"Reduced lower-extremity arterial perfusion, with an ABI below the normal range clinically supporting peripheral artery disease.","D":"Increased arterial perfusion because a lower ankle-to-brachial pressure ratio indicates less resistance to blood flow."}}
source_row.rationale: The ankle-brachial index compares blood pressure in the ankle to blood pressure in the arm; a low ABI value (generally below about 0.9) indicates reduced blood flow to the lower extremities, consistent with peripheral artery disease, helping confirm the diagnosis and assess severity.
source_row.source_detail: 2024 PAD guideline, Section 3.1 Resting ABI: ≤0.90 abnormal; 0.91–0.99 borderline; 1.00–1.40 normal; >1.40 noncompressible. JACC 2024; DOI 10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.013; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.

The nurse understands that a low ABI value instead generally indicates:

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Home INR testing removes the need for clinician review because the device automatically determines and changes the warfarin dose.","B":"Trained, selected clients can test INR at home, but results and warfarin management still require an agreed clinical follow-up plan.","C":"Home INR testing is intended for direct-acting oral anticoagulants rather than for clients receiving long-term warfarin therapy.","D":"Home INR testing is used only when standard laboratory INR testing is unavailable and is otherwise inappropriate for warfarin therapy."}}
source_row.rationale: Home INR self-testing devices allow eligible, appropriately trained and selected clients on long-term warfarin therapy to monitor their own INR more conveniently and potentially more frequently, which for suitable candidates may improve anticoagulation control, though results should still be communicated to and reviewed with the healthcare provider for dose management decisions.
source_row.source_detail: FDA home INR guidance: know target INR and testing schedule, contact provider for out-of-range results, and periodically compare meter results with a laboratory method. Current FDA device guidance reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.

source_row.stem: A client on long-term warfarin therapy is being considered for home INR self-testing, and initially assumes this would mean never needing to communicate with the provider about their results again. The nurse should explain that this option instead:

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Steady state is reached after exactly one half-life for essentially all medications, so the first routine dose provides a representative concentration.","B":"Steady state is often approached after about 4 to 5 half-lives, but the exact sampling time and target are drug-specific and follow the monitoring protocol.","C":"Steady-state sampling is required only for intravenous medications, because oral medications reach a stable concentration immediately after administration.","D":"A level drawn at any random time after several doses is equivalent to a correctly timed level, regardless of the medication's pharmacokinetics or dosing interval."}}
source_row.rationale: For drugs with linear pharmacokinetics, steady state is commonly approached after about 4 to 5 half-lives. Therapeutic drug monitoring remains drug-specific: the appropriate sample time (for example, trough or peak), target range, loading strategy, and clinical context determine when a level should be obtained.
source_row.source_detail: StatPearls Elimination Half-Life, steady-state section: regular dosing or continuous infusion reaches approximate steady state after about 4–5 half-lives, with pharmacokinetic caveats. StatPearls updated 2025-05-03; reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: Clinical Pharmacokinetics References — Steady State Concept
source_row.stem: A nurse is planning therapeutic drug monitoring for a medication that is usually measured after steady state is reached. Which explanation is most accurate?

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Right prescriber identity, meaning the nurse verifies that the ordering clinician is physically present before each dose is given.","B":"Right insurance authorization, meaning coverage must be confirmed before any scheduled medication can be administered safely.","C":"Right documentation and right reason, which are commonly included in expanded medication-administration safety frameworks today.","D":"Right room number, meaning the client's assigned location is used as an additional identifier before medication administration."}}
source_row.rationale: Beyond the traditional five rights (patient, drug, dose, route, time), expanded frameworks commonly include additional rights such as right documentation (recording administration accurately) and right reason (understanding the rationale/indication for the medication), reflecting a more comprehensive approach to medication safety.
source_row.source_detail: AHRQ PSNet primer, Five Rights section: five rights alone do not ensure medication safety; expanded rights include documentation, action/reason, form, and response. Current AHRQ PSNet primer reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: ISMP — Expanded Rights of Medication Administration
source_row.stem: A nurse is reviewing the expanded "rights" of medication administration with a nursing student, beyond the traditional five. Which additional "right" is commonly included in expanded frameworks?

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Fasting eliminates all gastric contents before anesthesia, so any aspiration cannot occur once the client has followed the required fasting interval.","B":"Fasting is used mainly to prevent postoperative nausea, and the same nothing-by-mouth interval applies to every type of food and clear liquid.","C":"Fasting reduces gastric contents available for regurgitation and aspiration; the required interval varies with intake and individual patient factors.","D":"Fasting is intended mainly to improve surgical exposure, while the risk of pulmonary aspiration is largely unrelated to recent oral intake."}}
source_row.rationale: Preoperative fasting is used to reduce the risk and potential severity of pulmonary aspiration of gastric contents during anesthesia. Fasting recommendations are not a single universal 'NPO after midnight' rule; the interval varies by the type of intake and the patient's clinical circumstances.
source_row.source_detail: ASA 2023 modular update to preoperative fasting guidelines: fasting recommendations for healthy patients undergoing elective procedures are designed to reduce pulmonary aspiration risk and distinguish clear liquids from solids. Anesthesiology 2023; DOI 10.1097/ALN.0000000000004381; reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: American Society of Anesthesiologists — Preoperative Fasting Guidelines
source_row.stem: A client scheduled for anesthesia asks why preprocedure fasting instructions are necessary. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The crutch pad is about 1 to 1.5 inches below the axilla, the elbows are slightly flexed, and body weight is supported through the hands only.","B":"The crutch pad is pressed firmly into the axilla, the elbows remain fully extended, and most body weight is supported through the armpits.","C":"The crutch pad is level with the axilla, the handgrips are set below wrist level, and body weight is transferred through the axillary pads.","D":"The crutch pad is several inches above the axilla, the elbows are locked straight, and forward movement is produced by leaning on the armpits."}}
source_row.rationale: Axillary crutches are fitted with space between the axilla and the crutch pad—about 1 to 1.5 inches (roughly two to three finger widths)—with slight elbow flexion. Body weight should be borne through the hands, not the axillae, to reduce neurovascular compression.
source_row.source_detail: MedlinePlus Using Crutches, fitting instructions: top of crutch 1–1.5 inches below armpit; support weight on hands rather than armpits. NIH MedlinePlus current patient instructions reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: Standard Nursing Fundamentals — Proper Crutch Fitting and Use
source_row.stem: A nurse is fitting a client for axillary crutches. Which finding indicates an appropriate fit and weight-bearing technique?

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Keep the room dark and minimize all conversation throughout the day so the client receives as little stimulation as possible between nursing procedures.","B":"Use continuous television and frequent waking overnight to provide stimulation, even when the client is sleeping or does not want additional activity.","C":"Avoid clocks, calendars, hearing aids, and family interaction because orientation cues can increase confusion in clients who are critically ill.","D":"Use a multicomponent delirium-prevention approach with reorientation, sleep support, mobility as appropriate, and access to hearing or vision aids."}}
source_row.rationale: ICU delirium prevention is multicomponent rather than based on either sensory deprivation or indiscriminate stimulation. Measures include regular reorientation, sleep promotion, early mobility when appropriate, and correction of sensory impairment with hearing or vision aids.
source_row.source_detail: SCCM PADIS nonpharmacologic delirium recommendation: multicomponent intervention targeting cognition, sleep, mobility, hearing and vision, including reorientation and sensory aids. 2018 PADIS with 2025 focused update/current SCCM listing; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: Standard Nursing Fundamentals — Sensory Deprivation Prevention in Critical Care
source_row.stem: An older adult in the ICU is at risk for delirium and has limited mobility, disrupted sleep, and impaired hearing. Which nursing approach is most appropriate?

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Calcium has little physiologic role in adult bone because skeletal mineralization is essentially complete once a person reaches early adulthood.","B":"Calcium supplements should routinely exceed the recommended intake because higher doses consistently provide greater fracture prevention for all adults.","C":"Vitamin D and physical activity make dietary calcium unnecessary, because bone mineral can be maintained without an adequate calcium supply.","D":"Adequate calcium is needed for normal bone mineralization and maintenance, while intake should generally meet age-appropriate recommendations."}}
source_row.rationale: Calcium is a major structural component of bone and adequate intake supports normal bone mineralization and maintenance. Recommended intake varies by age and life stage; routinely exceeding recommended amounts is not a substitute for individualized nutrition and bone-health assessment.
source_row.source_detail: NIH ODS Calcium fact sheet, Health Effects/Bone health section: calcium is central to bone structure; low intake contributes to osteoporosis risk, while supplementation outcomes depend on context. Current NIH ODS fact sheet reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: National Osteoporosis Foundation / NIH — Calcium and Bone Health Across the Lifespan
source_row.stem: A nurse provides health-promotion teaching about calcium and bone health. Which statement is most accurate?

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Adequate folic acid for all women, since defects occur early","B":"Folic acid being unnecessary unless actively trying to conceive","C":"Folic acid supplementation only after pregnancy is confirmed","D":"Folic acid only for women with a family history of defects"}}
source_row.rationale: Because neural tube development occurs very early in pregnancy (often before a woman even realizes she is pregnant), the CDC and other health organizations recommend that all women of childbearing age who could become pregnant consume adequate folic acid, rather than waiting until pregnancy is confirmed, to help reduce the risk of neural tube defects.
source_row.source_detail: CDC folic-acid recommendation: all women capable of becoming pregnant should get 400 mcg folic acid daily to help prevent neural tube defects. CDC page current 2026-06-02; reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: CDC — Folic Acid Recommendations for Women of Childbearing Age
source_row.stem: A nurse is providing health promotion education to a group of women of childbearing age, regardless of current pregnancy status or plans. The nurse should recommend:

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"At least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity each week, with no need for regular activity on most other days.","B":"At least 30 minutes of light physical activity each day, with muscle- and bone-strengthening activity avoided until adulthood.","C":"At least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity daily, including aerobic and age-appropriate strengthening activities.","D":"The same 150-minutes-per-week target used for adults, because children and adolescents do not have a separate activity guideline today."}}
source_row.rationale: The CDC recommends that children and adolescents (ages 6-17) engage in at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity daily, including a variety of aerobic, muscle-strengthening, and bone-strengthening activities throughout the week, to support healthy growth, development, and long-term health.
source_row.source_detail: CDC child activity guideline: ages 6–17 need ≥60 min/day moderate-to-vigorous activity; vigorous and muscle-strengthening activity at least 3 days/week, with bone-strengthening activity also 3 days/week. CDC page updated 2025-12-04; reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: CDC — Physical Activity Guidelines for Children and Adolescents
source_row.stem: A nurse is providing health promotion teaching to a parent about physical activity recommendations for their school-age child. Per CDC guidelines, children and adolescents should generally get:

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Minimize distractions, use attentive posture, reflect or paraphrase the client's words, and adapt eye contact to the client's own cultural preference and comfort.","B":"Maintain prolonged direct eye contact throughout the exchange even if the client looks away, because active listening requires the same nonverbal behavior in every culture.","C":"Interrupt frequently with advice so the client knows the nurse is engaged, while avoiding pauses that could allow the client to describe concerns in more detail.","D":"Focus on preparing the next response while the client is speaking, because quickly offering solutions is more important than checking the nurse's understanding."}}
source_row.rationale: Active listening includes focused attention, minimizing distractions, reflective responses, and checking understanding. Nonverbal behaviors such as eye contact should be culturally responsive and individualized rather than treated as a universal requirement.
source_row.source_detail: AHRQ TeamSTEPPS Communication section: effective communication is respectful and requires attention/verification; nonverbal expectations such as eye contact vary across cultural backgrounds. Current TeamSTEPPS 3.0 page reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: Standard Nursing Fundamentals — Active Listening Communication Techniques
source_row.stem: A nurse is using active listening with a distressed client from a cultural background in which prolonged direct eye contact may be uncomfortable. Which behavior best demonstrates active listening?

source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use the nurse's own explanatory model consistently so treatment decisions are not altered by differing cultural beliefs about mental illness.","B":"Explore the client's beliefs and preferences, incorporate them into collaborative care when feasible, and avoid stereotyping the individual.","C":"Assume clients from the same cultural group share the same beliefs, then select treatment according to the group's expected preferences.","D":"Avoid discussing cultural beliefs because biomedical treatment is most effective when personal explanatory models are excluded from care."}}
source_row.rationale: Culturally sensitive mental health care includes understanding and respecting the client's own cultural beliefs about mental illness, its causes, and appropriate treatment approaches (which may differ significantly across cultures), integrating this understanding into a collaborative, individualized care approach — while also recognizing individual variation within any cultural group rather than assuming uniformity.
source_row.source_detail: National CLAS Standards, Principal Standard: respectful, understandable, quality care responsive to cultural health beliefs/practices, preferred languages, health literacy, and other communication needs. Current HHS Think Cultural Health standards reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: APA — Cultural Competence in Mental Health Care Guidelines
source_row.stem: A nurse is providing mental health care to a client whose cultural background has different beliefs about mental illness than the nurse's own, and the nurse initially wonders whether it would be simpler to just apply their own clinical framework rather than navigate the difference. Culturally sensitive care instead includes:
